Season snow total

The side bet: how many inches of snow State College gets this winter. The closest guess to the official season total wins.

Rules: every inch measured at the official State College weather station (the same one First Flakes uses) counts. The season normally wraps up April 30, but it stays open through May 15 in case a late storm shows up, so any snow through May 15 counts. Identical guesses share the win, and so do two guesses exactly the same distance from the final total.

What's driving this forecast

How it works: the season total so far is the official count at the State College weather station. The rest of the season is built from what State College's last 35 winters (1991-92 to 2025-26) got over the same dates, every winter counting equally, each one scaled for State College's long-term decline in snowfall (about 18% less per decade since 1991). Tested against all 35 winters, and forward in time on every winter since 2006-07, that scored better than unscaled winters, and weighting recent winters more did worse. For the next 10 days the forecast takes over: the National Blend of Models and the European model's expected snow, trusted fully for the next few days and blended back toward the 35-winter average farther out. CPC's 6-10 and 8-14 day outlooks nudge the two weeks after that. Thousands of simulated finishes give each guess its chance of being closest; identical guesses, and two guesses the same distance from the final total, share the win.

What's driving this forecast

Model inputs

Every forecast product that fed this update, and how much it moved the daily snow chance.

SourceCoversWhat it saysEffect

How it works: the starting curve comes from State College's actual first-flake dates for 1991–2025 (NOAA records), shifted for the warming trend of about 2 days later per decade, and checked by predicting each past year from the others. The forecast updates twice a day, at about 5:15 AM and 5:15 PM, right after the newest European, GFS, National Blend, NWS and CPC forecasts come out; the evening update keeps the morning headline unless something changed significantly. Days still turn over at midnight Eastern: once a day passes with no flakes, it drops out of the odds right away and the remaining days rescale until the morning update. For the next 10 days, a weighted consensus of forecast models replaces the curve: the National Blend of Models (60%, itself a calibrated blend of about 30 models including the European, American and Canadian ensembles and the HRRR), GFS MOS (30%, out to 8 days), the European model (15%, ECMWF's main run read straight from its open data, out to 10 days; it has no MOS, so its chance comes from its own rain, snowfall and temperatures and fades toward normal farther out), the high-resolution NAM (10%, out to 3½ days, until NWS retires it) and LAMP (10%, the hourly-updated guidance for the next day, newest run), each turned into a daily chance of flakes from its chance of precipitation and chance of snow. Past that, CPC's outlooks nudge it up or down: the 6-10 and 8-14 day temperature and precipitation outlooks, the week 3-4 temperature outlook, and the Day 8-14 Hazards Outlook (a flagged risk of much below-normal cold raises the chance further, and also lifts the model blend's far days, 7 or more days out, where the blend tends to smooth away sharp cold shots), with smooth handoffs between forecasts. Closer in, WPC's Day 3-7 Hazards Outlook counts too: heavy snow flagged over State College sets that day's chance to at least 30%. El Niño gets no adjustment: State College's strong El Niño falls haven't run later. The same goes for how warm the fall has run and the AO, NAO and PNA patterns: each shows on its own card, but in 35 years of State College records none of them, known ahead of time, reliably moved the first flakes, and the pattern signals for the coming weeks are already inside CPC's outlooks. Each pick is then scored by how often it would be the closest guess, with same-date picks sharing the win in full and a day exactly halfway between two picks split at noon (half that day's chance to each side).
